a: The word of blessing of Enoch
p: The book begins the way Deuteronomy 33 begins: a blessing spoken before the end.
b: Deuteronomy 33:1 introduces Moses' last words: "This is the blessing." 1 Enoch opens the same way, and in 1:4 God comes from Sinai, as in Deuteronomy 33:2. The writer presents Enoch, who lived long before Moses, speaking in Moses' voice. Many scholars think this is deliberate: the book claims an authority that is older than Sinai but agrees with it. The Greek and the Ge'ez both say "word of blessing," and in the Greek the blessed are the "chosen righteous."

a: the chosen and the righteous
t: "The chosen": the book's name for its readers
p: Ḫəruyan, "the chosen," is how the Enoch writings name the faithful group they write for.
b: The Ge'ez ḫəruyan (Greek eklektoi) and ṣadqan name the people the book is written for. "The chosen" runs through all five parts of 1 Enoch. In the Parables the singular becomes a title, "the Chosen One" (see 39:6). The group that copied these books seems to have seen itself as a faithful few inside Israel, waiting for a day of trouble when God would sort the righteous from the wicked.

a: the day of trouble
p: Ge'ez "day of distress," Greek "day of necessity": the crisis before the judgment.
b: Məndabe means distress or affliction; the Greek has anankē, "necessity, hard pressure." The phrase echoes the prophets' "day of trouble" (Zephaniah 1:15) and Daniel's "a time of distress ... with no equal" (Daniel 12:1). The Greek says the day comes "to remove all the enemies," where the Ge'ez has "the evil and the wicked."

a: whose eyes God had opened
p: "Took up his message" and "whose eyes were opened" borrow Balaam's oracle formula.
b: Numbers 24:3–4 introduces Balaam's oracle: "Then he took up his poem and said" and calls him the one who "sees what the Almighty shows" with "eyes uncovered." The Greek of 1 Enoch 1:2 uses the same word as the Greek of Numbers, parabolē. Balaam also said of his vision, "I see him, but not yet" (Numbers 24:17), and Enoch says his vision is for a distant generation. Both are outsiders to Israel's later history who see its end.

a: The angels showed it to me
p: The verse starts by speaking about Enoch, then Enoch himself takes over.
b: Both the Ge'ez and the Greek switch in mid-sentence from "he saw" to "the angels showed me." The Plain keeps the switch. A narrator introduces Enoch, and then Enoch speaks for himself for the rest of the book. The same shift happens again at 12:3 and 13:1–3.

a: It was not for this generation, but for a distant generation still to come
p: Enoch says his vision is for people far in the future. 1 Peter says the same of the prophets.
b: The book explains why an ancient man's words reach readers so late: they were meant for the final generation, the book's real first readers. Daniel is told to seal up his words until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). Agrees in idea: 1 Peter 1:10–12 says the prophets served "not themselves but you." Differs: Daniel and 1 Peter speak of prophets whose books Israel kept from their own day; 1 Enoch claims a pre-Flood author, which most scholars and most churches do not accept (see the book's opening pages).

a: The Holy Great One
p: The Book of the Watchers' favorite name for God.
b: Qədus wäʿabiy (Greek ho hagios ho megas) joins Isaiah's "Holy One of Israel" with "the Great One." It is the usual name for God in chapters 1–36 (10:1; 14:1; 25:3) and returns in the Epistle (see 92:2). The site renders it the same way in every part of 1 Enoch.

a: will come out from his dwelling
p: Micah 1:3–4 is the model: God comes out, treads on the heights, and mountains melt.
b: Micah 1:3–4 pictures the LORD coming out of his place, treading on the high places of the earth, while mountains melt like wax before fire. 1:3–6 follows the same order: God comes out, treads on Sinai, mountains shake and melt (1:6). Isaiah 26:21 has the same picture of God coming out of his place to punish the earth.

a: on Mount Sinai
p: The last judgment is pictured as a new Sinai, as in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3.
b: Old poems picture God marching from Sinai to save his people (Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3). 1 Enoch turns the march into the final judgment: the God who gave the covenant at Sinai comes back to judge by it. This matters because the Book of the Watchers rarely mentions Moses or the law. Scholars debate whether the Enoch groups set Enoch beside Moses or above him; this verse at least places their hope at Sinai.

a: his camp
p: Təʿyənt, Greek parembolē: a camp, and so an army in camp.
b: The Ge'ez təʿyənt and the Greek parembolē both mean a military camp. God comes with his army, the heavenly host of 1:9. Jacob called the place where he met angels "God's camp" (Genesis 32:2).

a: The Watchers
p: Ge'ez təguhan, Greek egrēgoroi, Aramaic 'irin: "those who are awake."
b: The name comes from the Aramaic 'irin, "wakeful ones," angels who never sleep. Daniel 4:13, 17 and 23 speak of "a watcher, a holy one" coming down from heaven. In 1 Enoch the word can mean the angels in general (12:2; 20:1), but usually it means the two hundred who came down to earth (6:1–8). Here, at the start, they shake with fear before the coming judge. The Greek of this line is confused: Charles printed it with words that seem to say the Watchers "will believe" and "sing hidden things," and bracketed them as additions.

a: They will melt like wax in front of a flame
p: A stock picture of God's coming in the Psalms and the prophets.
b: "Like wax, the mountains melt away in the LORD's presence" (Psalm 97:5) and "like wax near a fire" (Micah 1:4). Judges 5:5 has the mountains quake before the God of Sinai. The Ge'ez literally says "like a honeycomb," the wax of the comb.

a: on all the righteous too
p: Only the Ge'ez says the righteous are judged here; the Greek stops at "everyone."
b: The Greek reads "judgment will be against all," and then 1:8 begins, "and with the righteous he will make peace." The Ge'ez adds "and on all the righteous," probably by repeating the next line. Read as it stands, the Ge'ez makes a fair point: everyone stands before the judge, and the righteous receive peace from that same judgment (compare 2 Corinthians 5:10).

a: God's light will shine on them
p: Peace, guarding, mercy and shining light: the words of Aaron's blessing.
b: Numbers 6:24–26 asks the LORD to bless, guard, make his face shine, show grace and give peace. 1:8 promises the same gifts to the chosen at the judgment: peace, protection, mercy, blessing and light. The judgment that destroys the wicked is the priestly blessing fulfilled for the righteous.

a: Look! He has come
t: "He has come": a past tense for the future
p: The Ge'ez, like Jude 14, uses a past tense; the Greek of 1 Enoch has "he comes."
b: The Ge'ez mäṣʾä is a perfect, "he came," and Jude 14 also has a past tense, ēlthen. The surviving Greek of 1 Enoch has the present, erchetai. Hebrew and Aramaic prophets often describe a sure future event as if it were already done, and many scholars think Jude's past tense reflects that Semitic idiom, perhaps from the Aramaic original. Jude also has "the Lord," which neither the Ge'ez nor the Greek has here; in 1 Enoch the one who comes is God himself (1:3–4).
orig: ናሁ መጽአ (nahu mäṣʾä); ἔρχεται (erchetai); Jude 14 ἦλθεν (ēlthen)

a: ten thousands of holy ones
p: Deuteronomy 33:2 and Zechariah 14:5 stand behind "ten thousands of holy ones."
b: Moses' blessing says the LORD "came from among ten thousands of holy ones" (Deuteronomy 33:2), and Zechariah 14:5 says, "the LORD my God will arrive, and all the holy ones will be with you." In all three the holy ones are angels. When Christians read Jude 14, some took them to be the saints who come with Christ (1 Thessalonians 3:13), but in 1 Enoch they are clearly the angelic host.

a: to carry out judgment on all
p: Jude 14–15 quotes this verse and calls it Enoch's prophecy: the only such quotation in the Bible.
b: Jude 14–15 is the one place where a book of the 66 quotes 1 Enoch by name, and it uses the verb "prophesied." How churches read it: the Ethiopian Orthodox churches take it as proof that the book is a true prophecy and belongs in the Bible. Tertullian argued the same way (On the Apparel of Women 1.3). Jerome reports that many rejected Jude because of the quotation, and Augustine said Jude's use shows Enoch wrote something inspired, not that this whole book is Enoch's (City of God 15.23). Most Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teachers say that quoting a true sentence from a book does not make the book Scripture, as Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12).

a: convict all flesh
p: Ge'ez təwaqäs and Greek elenchō mean to prove someone guilty, not only to scold.
b: Elenchō is a courtroom word: to bring a charge home with evidence. The Ge'ez täwaqäsä also means to argue a case against someone. The Greek and the Ge'ez say "all flesh," that is, every human being. Jude 15 has "all the ungodly" in most manuscripts, but "every person" (literally "every soul") in Papyrus 72 and Codex Sinaiticus, the reading the NA28 prints, which is closer to Enoch's "all flesh."
orig: ወይትዋቀስ ኵሎ ዘሥጋ (wäytəwaqäs kʷilo zäśga); ἐλέγξει πᾶσαν σάρκα (elenxei pasan sarka)

a: none of them breaks its command
p: The lesson of 2:1–5:3 is the contrast in 5:4: everything keeps God's order except you.
b: The sun, moon and stars keep their times; trees and seas do their work. Jeremiah makes the same contrast: the sea stays inside its limits, but this people has a rebellious heart (Jeremiah 5:22–23), and the stork knows its seasons, but Israel does not know the LORD's rules (Jeremiah 8:7). The Testament of Naphtali 3:2–5 later uses the same argument against the Watchers. The Greek adds that the lights appear "at their festivals": keeping the right calendar was a deep concern for the Enoch groups (see 72:1).

a: except fourteen trees
p: Why fourteen is not known. The point is that even the exceptions follow a fixed rule.
b: In the eastern Mediterranean most trees lose their leaves or look dead in the dry season and in winter, while a few, such as olive, cedar, cypress, laurel and pine, keep theirs. The Ethiopian manuscripts agree on the number fourteen, but no list of the fourteen survives. The Greek manuscript of this passage is damaged and shorter.

a: you cannot walk on the earth or on a rock
p: In the hills of Judea and Galilee, summer rock is too hot to stand on barefoot.
b: The writer appeals to what every farmer and shepherd in Judea knew. From June to September no rain falls, the sun stands high, and the people seek shade at midday. Even this harsh heat comes at its fixed time, which is the point of the lesson.

a: the One who lives forever
p: A title for God from Daniel and the Psalms, later used in Revelation.
b: Zäḥəyaw läʿaläm, "who lives forever," names God as the one whose life does not run out, unlike every creature in 2:1–5:3. Daniel 12:7 has an angel swear "by the one who lives forever," and Revelation 4:9–10 uses the same title for the one on the throne.

a: proud and harsh words
p: The sin 1 Enoch names first is speech: the same charge Jude makes.
b: The Greek has "great and hard words," the pair that the Aramaic of 1:9 also has as Milik read it; 27:2 has "hard things" and 101:3 returns to the theme. Jude takes it up: his quotation, like the Greek of 1:9, ends with the harsh words ungodly sinners spoke against him (Jude 15), and the next verse says the false teachers' mouths speak puffed-up words (Jude 16). The Ge'ez "against his greatness" is the Greek megalōsynē, majesty.

a: You hard-hearted people
p: Ge'ez "dry of heart"; Greek sklērokardioi, "hard of heart."
b: The Ge'ez yəbusanä ləb means literally "dry of heart," a heart that has lost its life. The Greek sklērokardioi is the word Jesus uses for the stubborn (Mark 10:5; Matthew 19:8) and that the Greek Old Testament uses in Deuteronomy 10:16. The phrase ties the speech sin to its source.

a: you will have no peace
p: The verdict on the wicked and on the Watchers, repeated through the book.
b: "You will have no peace" returns at 12:5, 13:1 and 16:4 for the Watchers, and many times in the Epistle (see 94:6; 98:11). It goes back to Isaiah: "There is no peace for the wicked" (Isaiah 48:22; Isaiah 57:21). In Hebrew thought peace (shalom) is wholeness with God and the world, so "no peace" is the opposite of salvation.

a: you will make your names an everlasting curse
p: 5:4–9 is built on Isaiah 65, where the wicked leave their name as a curse for God's chosen.
b: Isaiah 65:15 tells the rebels they will leave their name for God's chosen to use as a curse, while the chosen inherit the land, live long and do not labor in vain (Isaiah 65:9, 20–23). 1 Enoch 5:6–9 follows the same points in order: names as a curse, the chosen inherit the earth, long life, no early death. The Greek of 5:6 is much longer and repeats the blessing on the chosen (see the variants).

a: they will inherit the earth
t: The meek and the chosen inherit the earth
p: Psalm 37, 1 Enoch and Jesus' beatitude share one promise.
b: Psalm 37:11 promises that the humble will inherit the land, and Jesus repeats it: the gentle "will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). Agrees: 1 Enoch makes the same promise to the chosen. Goes beyond: 1 Enoch spells out the inheritance as long earthly life after the wicked are removed (5:9; 10:17), while the New Testament joins the promise to the resurrection and a new creation (Revelation 21:1–4). Christians read the beatitude through Jesus; Jewish readers through the land promise.

a: Then wisdom will be given to the chosen
t: Wisdom as the gift of the end
p: In 1 Enoch, true wisdom is revealed at the end, and this book claims to be that wisdom.
b: Wisdom here is not cleverness but knowing God's ways and keeping them. The Greek adds that "there will be light in the enlightened person." Later parts say the wise will receive Enoch's books (see 82:2–3; 104:12–13). The book thus offers itself as the wisdom of the last days, in contrast to the stolen knowledge the Watchers taught (8:1–3).

a: They will grow old in peace
t: A long life, not yet eternal life
p: The Book of the Watchers promises long, peaceful lives on earth, as Isaiah 65 does.
b: Agrees with Isaiah: Isaiah 65:20–22 promises no infant deaths and lives as long as a tree's. The Book of the Watchers pictures the same: the righteous live out their full days and die in peace (also 10:17; 25:6). Differs from later texts: Daniel 12:2, later parts of 1 Enoch (see 104:2–6) and the New Testament speak of resurrection to everlasting life (John 5:28–29; 1 Corinthians 15:52–54). The book shows a stage in Jewish hope before the resurrection became the main picture.

a: In those days, when human beings had become many
p: Four puzzling verses of Genesis become a whole story.
b: Genesis 6:1–4 says only that "the sons of God saw that the daughters of humankind were good to look at" (Genesis 6:2), took wives, and that the Nephilim were on earth. 1 Enoch 6–11 tells who these sons of God were, how many, where they came down, what they taught and how they were punished. Most scholars think the Enoch story expands Genesis. Milik argued the reverse, that Genesis 6:1–4 shortens an older Enoch story; few have followed him, but both texts clearly drew on a shared tradition.

a: The angels, the children of heaven
p: 1 Enoch settles Genesis's question: they were angels. Later readers disagreed.
b: Genesis says "sons of God"; 1 Enoch says "angels, children of heaven," and Syncellus's Greek says "the Watchers." Views of Genesis 6:2: (1) Angels, the reading of 1 Enoch, Jubilees, Philo, Josephus, and early Christian writers such as Justin and Irenaeus. (2) Sons of Seth, godly men who married women of Cain's line: Julius Africanus, Chrysostom and Augustine, later standard in the West. (3) Sons of rulers: Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai (Genesis Rabbah 26:5) and the Targums. Jesus' saying that angels do not marry (Matthew 22:30) is used on both sides.

a: Semyaza, their leader
p: The chief of the Watchers. The Aramaic scrolls spell him Shemihazah.
b: The Ge'ez has Səmyaza, the Greek Semiazas, and the Aramaic fragments from Qumran (4Q201, 4Q202) Shemihazah. The name probably means "my name has seen" or "the Name (God) has seen," a bitter name for one who led a rebellion God saw. The Plain uses the Ge'ez form, Semyaza, in all parts of 1 Enoch.

a: I alone will have to pay for this great sin
t: A sin they knew was sin
p: The angels call it "a great sin" before they commit it, and bind each other by oath.
b: In Genesis the sons of God simply take wives. In 1 Enoch they plan it, name it a great sin, and swear an oath so no one will back out (6:4–5). The fall is not a mistake but a conspiracy. The Greek calls Semyaza the one who will be "a debtor" of a great sin: sin as a debt that must be paid.

a: in the days of Jared
p: Jared's name sounds like Hebrew yarad, "go down": they came down in the days of "Descent."
b: Jared was Enoch's father (Genesis 5:18). His name in Hebrew, Yered, sounds like yarad, "to go down," and Jubilees 4:15 also says the angels came down in his days, though there they come to teach justice and only later sin. Later in 1 Enoch, Enoch recalls that "in the days of Jared my father" some angels broke God's word (see 106:13). The Plain follows the Greek of Syncellus here; the Ge'ez has "on Ardis" (see the variant).

a: Mount Hermon
p: The highest mountain of the land, sacred to many peoples, at the northern edge of Israel.
b: Mount Hermon (about 9,200 feet) rises over the springs of the Jordan on today's Lebanon–Syria–Israel border. The Bible calls it Senir and Sirion (Deuteronomy 3:9) and Baal-hermon (Judges 3:3; 1 Chronicles 5:23), a sign of the god once worshiped there; remains of many temples from the Greek and Roman period stand on its slopes. Placing the Watchers' oath there tied the mountain's pagan holiness to the angels' rebellion. Enoch himself goes near it to read their petition (13:7).

a: bound one another with curses
p: A pun: Hermon sounds like ḥerem, "something put under a curse."
b: The Greek anathematizō and the Ge'ez ʾäwgäzä mean to bind with a curse: "may I be cursed if I break this oath." In Hebrew and Aramaic the root ḥrm means to put under a ban or curse (ḥerem), and it sounds like Hermon. The story explains the mountain's name: the place of the curse-oath. The pun works only in Hebrew or Aramaic, one sign that the book was first written in Aramaic.

a: These are the names of their leaders
p: The Ethiopic names are worn down by copying; the Aramaic keeps older forms built on nature words.
b: Each name ends in -el, "God," and in the Aramaic most begin with a piece of nature: Kokabel "star of God," Baraqel "lightning of God," Shamsiel "sun of God," Sahriel "moon of God," as Milik and Nickelsburg read the fragments. That fits 8:3, where they teach star-lore and signs. The Ge'ez list has nineteen names, the Gizeh Greek twenty-one and Syncellus twenty, all spelled differently (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Ge'ez forms but uses one spelling for the angels named again in 8:1–3: Kokabel, Baraqel, Azazel and Armaros.

a: These are the chiefs of the two hundred angels
p: The Greek calls them "chiefs of ten": twenty leaders, each over ten angels.
b: The Gizeh Greek reads dekarchoi, "leaders of tens," and adds "and all the rest with them." The Ge'ez says "chiefs of the two hundred angels." The two agree in sense: twenty chiefs times ten makes two hundred. The army-like order mirrors Israel's camp, with officers over tens (Exodus 18:21).

a: they began to go to them and sleep with them
p: 1 Enoch says plainly what Genesis 6 leaves open. Christians still disagree about it.
b: Goes beyond: Genesis 6:2 does not say that the sons of God were angels or that their sin was crossing a boundary God set. Agrees, many think: Jude 6–7 says the angels left their own dwelling and that Sodom, "in the same way," went after "other flesh"; 2 Peter 2:4–5 sets the angels beside the Flood. Seems to conflict, others think: Jesus says that in the resurrection "men do not take wives and women are not given as wives. They are like God's angels in heaven" (Matthew 22:30). Ethiopian Orthodox teachers accept the angel reading; Augustine and most later Western teachers rejected it; many modern evangelical and Catholic scholars now think Jude meant it.

a: potions and spells and the cutting of roots
p: In the ancient world, herbal medicine and magic were one craft.
b: The Greek has pharmakeia, epaoidai and rhizotomia: drugs, chants and root-cutting. Greek "root-cutters" gathered plants for medicine and for spells. 1 Enoch traces this whole craft to the fallen angels. Jubilees 10:10–13 tells a different story: an angel teaches Noah healing herbs so he can fight the evil spirits. The Bible forbids sorcery (Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and Paul lists pharmakeia among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20).

a: huge giants
p: The Greek Old Testament already called the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 "giants."
b: Genesis 6:4 speaks of the Nephilim and the gibborim, "the heroes of ancient times." The Septuagint translated both with gigantes, and the Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch use gibborin. The Ge'ez räʿayt follows the Greek. Syncellus's Greek says the women bore three races: giants, who fathered Nephilim, who fathered the Elioud. The Gizeh Greek of 9:9 even calls them "Titans," the giants of Greek myth.

a: The giants ate up everything people worked to produce
t: What did the giants stand for?
p: Scholars hear in the giants the wars of Alexander's successors, or a corrupt priesthood.
b: (1) Warlords. Nickelsburg reads the giants, born of "gods" and devouring the land, as a picture of the generals who fought over Judea after Alexander the Great died in 323 BC and called themselves sons of gods. (2) Priests. Suter read the angels who left their holy place to marry women as priests in Jerusalem who married outside the rules. (3) A story about evil's source. Hanson read chapters 6–11 as an old myth of heavenly rebellion. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read it as history from before the Flood.

a: drank the blood
p: Before the Flood the giants break the rule God gives Noah after it.
b: After the Flood God allows meat but forbids eating it with its lifeblood (Genesis 9:4); the law repeats the ban (Leviticus 17:10–14), and the apostles kept it for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29). The giants sin against every kind of creature and devour blood itself. In 1 Enoch the Flood is God's answer to bloodshed (9:1, 9), as Genesis 6:11 says the earth was filled with violence.

a: the earth brought a charge against the lawless ones
p: As Abel's blood cried from the ground, the earth itself brings a lawsuit.
b: God tells Cain, "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Isaiah 26:21 says the earth will uncover the blood shed on it. The Greek entynchanō is the word for bringing a case or petition before a ruler; it is used again for the souls who plead in 9:3 and 22:5–7, where Abel appears again.

a: Azazel
p: The Aramaic calls him Asael. The Ethiopic, like later tradition, links him to the Azazel of Leviticus 16.
b: In the Aramaic list the tenth Watcher is ʿAsael (the Ge'ez of 6:7 has Asael too, printed Azazel in the Plain), perhaps "God has made," and the Greek has Azaēl. The Ge'ez here and in 9:6, 10:4 and 13:1 writes ʾAzazʾel, the name of Leviticus 16, where one goat is chosen "for Azazel" (Leviticus 16:8) and sent into the wilderness carrying Israel's sins. The story in 10:4–8 seems built on that rite: Azazel is bound in the desert and all sin is written against him. Whether the writers already joined the two names or the Ethiopic made the link is debated.

a: swords, knives, shields and breastplates
p: In Greek myth Prometheus gives humans fire and crafts and is chained to a rock. Azazel is too.
b: The Greek Titan Prometheus stole fire for humans, taught them the arts, and was chained to a mountain rock as punishment (Hesiod; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound). Babylonian tradition told of wise apkallu who taught the arts of civilization before the Flood. Azazel teaches metalwork and is bound under jagged rocks (10:4–5). Verdict: the likeness is real and most scholars think the writers knew such stories, but they turn the culture hero into a villain. Genesis 4:22, by contrast, credits a man, Tubal-cain, with metalwork, with no blame.

a: eye paint
p: Antimony (kohl) darkened the eyes. The Bible links it with seduction.
b: The Greek stibeis is stibium, antimony powder used as dark eye shadow. Jezebel painted her eyes before Jehu (2 Kings 9:30), and the prophets picture faithless Jerusalem doing the same (Jeremiah 4:30; Ezekiel 23:40). 1 Enoch traces cosmetics to Azazel along with weapons: the arts of war and of seduction. Tertullian used this verse to argue that Christian women should not wear jewelry and makeup (On the Apparel of Women 1.2).

a: the changing of the world
p: A phrase found only in the Ethiopic; its meaning is unclear.
b: The Gizeh Greek ends the list with "dyes" and has nothing more. The Ge'ez adds täwlaṭä ʿaläm, "the change (or exchange) of the world." It may mean the arts that transform natural things, such as dyeing and metal-working, or it may come from a Greek line like Syncellus's report that people "transgressed and led the holy ones astray."

a: Baraqel taught the star-readers
p: 1 Enoch condemns the Watchers' astrology but gives Uriel's astronomy.
b: Astrology and omen-reading were Babylonian sciences, prized in the Greek world after Alexander. The Watchers teach "signs" and the moon's path (8:3), but later the angel Uriel shows Enoch the true laws of the sun, moon and stars (33:3; see 72:1). The difference is the source: knowledge stolen and taught for power, or knowledge God reveals so his people can keep his times.

a: their voice reached heaven
p: The pattern of the exodus and of Sodom: an outcry rises and God acts.
b: Israel's cry in Egypt went up to God (Exodus 2:23–25), and the outcry against Sodom reached him (Genesis 18:20–21). Syncellus's Greek gives the cry in words: "Bring our case before the Most High." In 9:3 the archangels repeat it.

a: Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel
p: The Bible names only Michael and Gabriel. Raphael comes from Tobit, Uriel from 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra.
b: Daniel names Gabriel (Daniel 8:16; 9:21) and Michael (Daniel 10:13; 12:1); Luke names Gabriel (Luke 1:19) and Jude calls Michael archangel (Jude 9). Raphael, "God heals," is the guide of Tobit, "one of the seven angels" (Tobit 12:15), and Uriel, "God is my light," explains secrets in 4 Ezra 4:1. The Aramaic fragment of this verse, as Milik read it, has Sariel in place of Uriel. Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Michael, Gabriel and Raphael; the Ethiopian Orthodox church also honors Uriel and others named in 1 Enoch.
r: Daniel 8:16; Daniel 10:13; Luke 1:19; Jude 9; Tobit 12:15; 4 Ezra 4:1; 20:1–8

a: Bring our case before the Most High
p: The archangels bring human cries to God. Churches differ on what that means for prayer.
b: Agrees: in Tobit 12:12, 15 Raphael brings Tobit's prayers before God, and in Revelation 8:3–4 an angel offers the saints' prayers with incense. Zechariah 1:12 shows an angel pleading for Jerusalem. Debated: Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and the Ethiopian church, ask angels to pray for them. Most Protestants say Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25) and that believers pray to God directly. 1 Enoch shows that the belief in angelic intercessors is older than Christianity.

a: You are Lord of lords, God of gods and King of kings
p: Titles from Deuteronomy and Daniel that Revelation gives to the Lamb.
b: Deuteronomy 10:17 calls the LORD "the God of gods and the Lord of lords"; Daniel 2:47 has "the God of gods and the lord of kings." Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 give "Lord of lords and King of kings" to the Lamb, and 1 Timothy 6:15 to God. The Greek of 9:4 has "King of those who rule," close to 1 Timothy's wording.

a: Everything lies uncovered and open before you
p: The same pair of words as Hebrews 4:13, "naked and laid open."
b: Hebrews 4:13 says all things are "naked and laid bare" to the eyes of the one we must answer to. The Greek of 1 Enoch 9:5 has phanera kai akalypta, "visible and uncovered." The prayer's point is pointed: if God sees everything, why has he not acted (9:11)?

a: the eternal secrets that were kept in heaven
p: The Watchers' crime was not only lust. It was taking heaven's secrets to earth.
b: Azazel "revealed the eternal secrets"; the Greek adds "which people strive to learn." The book sets two kinds of secret side by side: the stolen "worthless secret" of the Watchers (16:3), and the true mysteries God shows Enoch (see 103:2). Deuteronomy 29:29 draws a similar line between the secret things that belong to the LORD and the revealed things given to Israel.

a: the whole earth has been filled with blood and wrongdoing
p: The Watchers' story finds the root of the world's evil in angels, not in Adam alone.
b: Goes beyond: Genesis 6:11 says only that the earth was filled with violence. In 1 Enoch 6–16 the spread of violence, magic and sin comes from rebel angels and their giant sons; Adam's sin is barely mentioned (32:6). Contrasts: Paul traces sin and death to Adam (Romans 5:12), and James to each person's own desire (James 1:14). 1 Enoch itself later insists that people made sin themselves (see 98:4). Many readers hold both ideas: human guilt, and evil powers beyond us (Ephesians 6:12).

a: the souls of the dead are crying out
p: The cry of the murdered for justice, as in Revelation 6:9–10.
b: In Revelation 6:9–10 the souls of the slain cry, "How long, holy and true Master, until you judge?" 1 Enoch 9:10 and 22:5–7 picture the souls of the murdered pleading at heaven's gates until justice is done. Both draw on Abel's blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

a: yet you tell us nothing
p: The archangels ask the question of every age: you know, so why have you not acted?
b: The prayer is bold. God knows everything (9:5, 11) and yet the earth is full of blood. The angels do not know what God plans, much as Jesus says no angel knows the day (Mark 13:32) and 1 Peter 1:12 says angels long to look into the gospel. The book's answer comes at once in chapter 10: God has a plan, and he sends each archangel to act. Readers in a time of suffering are meant to find their own complaint here, and the answer.

a: the son of Lamech
p: The Flood is the first world judgment and a pattern of the last one.
b: Noah is never named in this chapter in the Ge'ez or Gizeh Greek; Syncellus adds "Go to Noah." The Flood clears the earth of the giants, and 10:16–11:2 jumps from the Flood to the final renewal. Jesus uses the same pattern: "The days of Noah show what the coming of the Son of Man will be like" (Matthew 24:37–39), and 2 Peter 3:5–7 sets the water of the Flood beside the coming fire. 1 Enoch tells Noah's birth in 106–107.

a: Hide yourself
p: The Ge'ez says "hide your head": take shelter.
b: Ḫəbaʾ rəʾsäkä, literally "hide your head," means take cover, keep yourself safe. The Greek has "hide yourself." The ark will be the hiding place. Isaiah 26:20 uses the same idea for God's people: "hide for just a moment until the fury goes past."

a: Bind Azazel hand and foot
p: The angels are chained in darkness until the judgment, exactly as Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 say.
b: Agrees closely: Jude 6 says the angels who left their dwelling are "kept in everlasting chains down in the gloom, for the judgment of the great day." 2 Peter 2:4 says God threw them into Tartarus in chains of gloom, kept for judgment. 1 Enoch has the same two steps: binding in darkness now (10:4–5, 12), fire on the great day (10:6, 13). Revelation 20:1–3 binds Satan in the abyss in a similar way. Most scholars think Jude and 2 Peter knew this story; some Protestant scholars think they used only common Jewish tradition. The manuscripts of 2 Peter 2:4 are split between "chains of gloom" and "pits of gloom" (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus); "pits" is closer still to 1 Enoch's prison under the hills and valleys of the earth (10:12).

a: Dudael
p: The desert prison may echo the place where the Azazel goat was pushed off a cliff.
b: Dudael (Greek Dadouēl) is not known on any map. The Mishnah says that the goat "for Azazel" was led into the Judean desert and pushed backward off a cliff (Mishnah Yoma 6:6), and it names the place where the goat was counted as having reached the wilderness Beit Ḥiddudo (Yoma 6:8). Many scholars see the same name behind Dudael, so Azazel's desert prison matches the end of the scapegoat rite (Leviticus 16:21–22). The link is a proposal, likely but not proven.

a: Cover his face so that he cannot see light
p: Jude's "gloom of darkness" for the rebels may come from here.
b: Jude 13 speaks of "wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever," and Jude 6 of chains "down in the gloom." Azazel is cast into darkness, covered with darkness, his face covered from the light. Jesus speaks of "the outer darkness" (Matthew 8:12; 22:13).

a: he will be thrown into the fire
t: Fire made ready for the devil and his angels
p: Jesus' "eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels" has the same order.
b: In Matthew 25:41 Jesus speaks of the "eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels," and Revelation 20:10 throws the devil into the lake of fire. 1 Enoch's fire for Azazel and the Watchers (10:6, 13; 21:7–10) is the earliest Jewish text we have that sets aside a fiery place of punishment for rebel angels.

a: Heal the earth
p: The healer angel is sent to heal the earth: a play on his name.
b: Raphael means "God heals" in Hebrew (rapha', to heal). In Tobit he heals Tobit's eyes (Tobit 3:17; 11:7–15). Here his task is to bind the one who ruined the earth and so heal it. The Ge'ez verb ʾaḥyawa means "make live, heal," and the Greek has iaomai, "heal."

a: Write down every sin against him
p: As the scapegoat carried Israel's sins into the desert, all sin is written on Azazel.
b: On the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses Israel's sins over the live goat and sends it to Azazel in the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21–22). Here the whole earth's ruin is blamed on Azazel's teaching. Christian readers have noticed the contrast with Christ, on whom the LORD laid the sins of us all (Isaiah 53:6; 1 Peter 2:24): the scapegoat carries sin away as a sign, Azazel is punished as its source.

a: the bastards
p: The Greek copies an Aramaic or Hebrew word, mamzer, a child of a forbidden union.
b: The Gizeh Greek has mazēreoi, a borrowed Semitic word: Hebrew mamzer (Deuteronomy 23:2) means a child of a forbidden union. The Ge'ez mänzəran keeps the borrowing. The giants are illegitimate because their fathers crossed the line between heaven and earth. The Dead Sea Scrolls' prayers against demons speak of "the spirits of the bastards" (4Q510), using the same word.

a: send them against one another
p: A Qumran book tells the giants' side: their dreams, their war and their fear of judgment.
b: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls are pieces of an Aramaic "Book of Giants" (1Q23–24, 4Q203, 4Q530–533, 6Q8). In it the giants, with names such as Ohyah and Hahyah, dream of their coming destruction, send to Enoch to explain the dreams, and one of them is named Gilgamesh, the hero of the Babylonian epic. The Manicheans later copied a version of it. It shows how widely the Watchers' story was told and expanded.

a: each of them hopes to live five hundred years
p: Genesis 6:3 limits human life to 120 years; the giants hope for 500.
b: Right after the sons of God take wives, the LORD says, "Their days will be 120 years" (Genesis 6:3). The giants, half heavenly, hope to live forever, or at least five hundred years. The Greek says their fathers' every desire will be refused. In this story mixing heaven and earth brings not longer life but early death in war.

a: bind them for seventy generations under the hills of the earth
p: 1 Peter 3:19–20 speaks of "spirits in prison" who disobeyed in Noah's day.
b: 1 Peter 3:19–20 says Christ went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed when God waited in the days of Noah. Views: (1) The Watchers. Many scholars (Dalton, Elliott) read it in the light of 1 Enoch: Christ announced his victory to the imprisoned angels, as Enoch announced their doom (13:1–10; 14:4–7). (2) Christ speaking through Noah to the people of his day (Augustine; Grudem). (3) Christ in the realm of the dead preaching to the human dead, the "harrowing of hell" of Catholic and Orthodox teaching. 1 Enoch makes view (1) natural, but does not settle it.

a: seventy generations
p: Seventy generations after Enoch brings Luke's family tree of Jesus to Jesus himself.
b: Enoch is seventh from Adam (60:8; Jude 14). Seventy generations after the Watchers are bound, judgment comes. Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:23–38) has seventy-seven names from God to Jesus, so Jesus stands seventy generations after Enoch. Richard Bauckham argued that Luke, or his source, shaped the list on purpose to show Jesus arriving at the end of 1 Enoch's seventy generations. Others think the number is a coincidence.

a: the depths of fire
p: The Greek says "the chaos of fire": the first picture of a fiery prison forever.
b: The Greek has to chaos tou pyros, "the abyss (chaos) of fire," together with torment and a prison "shut forever." Revelation's lake of fire (Revelation 20:10, 14–15) and the abyss (Revelation 20:1–3) are later forms of this picture. Enoch sees the place itself in 21:7–10.

a: the plant of righteousness and truth
p: God's people as a planting: a picture from Isaiah that the Enoch groups made their own.
b: Isaiah calls restored Israel "the sprout of my planting" (Isaiah 60:21) and "oaks of righteousness, the LORD's planting" (Isaiah 61:3). In the Apocalypse of Weeks Abraham is "the plant of righteous judgment" and the chosen are "the plant of truth" (see 93:2, 5, 10). The Damascus Document from Qumran says God caused "a root of planting" to sprout from Israel. Here, after the Flood, the plant is Noah's family and the righteous people who will come from it.

a: their sabbaths
p: Both the Ge'ez and the Greek say "sabbaths"; Charles thought it meant "old age."
b: The Greek ta sabbata autōn and the Ge'ez sänbätä ziʾähomu both say "their sabbaths." Charles suggested that a translator misread an Aramaic word for "old age" (the pair "youth and old age" would be natural). The Plain keeps the reading of both witnesses: the righteous will spend their working days and their sabbath rests in peace.
orig: ሰንበተ ዚአሆሙ (sänbätä ziʾähomu); τὰ σάββατα αὐτῶν (ta sabbata autōn)

a: a thousand measures for one
p: Early Christians took up this picture of huge harvests for Christ's kingdom on earth.
b: Amos 9:13 promises that the plowman will overtake the reaper. 2 Baruch 29:5 says one vine will have a thousand branches. Irenaeus reports that Papias, who said he learned it from those who knew the apostle John, taught that in the kingdom each vine would have ten thousand branches (Against Heresies 5.33.3–4). This is one road by which Enoch's hope reached Christian beliefs about a thousand-year reign.

a: All nations will worship and bless me
p: Even the Book of the Watchers looks for all peoples to worship Israel's God.
b: The prophets promised that the nations would stream to the LORD's mountain (Isaiah 2:2–4) and go up to worship the King (Zechariah 14:16). The Watchers' book, often called narrow, ends its Flood story with all humankind made righteous and all nations bowing to God. Revelation 15:4 sings the same: "All the nations will come ... and worship in front of you." Ethiopian Christians have long seen themselves among these nations (Psalm 68:31; Acts 8:27).

a: I will never again send a flood on it
p: God's promise to Noah, repeated for the renewed earth.
b: After the Flood God promises, "there will not again be a flood to ruin the earth" (Genesis 9:11). The Ge'ez names the flood, ʾäyḫ, as in 10:2; the Greek says only, "I will no longer send on them." Here the promise is stretched to the final, cleansed earth: never again punishment or torment.

a: Peace and truth will be partners
p: Psalm 85:10: loyal love and truth meet, righteousness and peace kiss.
b: Psalm 85:10–11 pictures God's virtues meeting and embracing in a restored land. The Greek of 11:2 says truth and peace "will share together," a word for business partners. 11:1 also echoes Deuteronomy 28:12: the LORD will open his good storehouse, the sky, to bless the work of your hands.

a: Enoch had been hidden
p: Genesis says God "took" Enoch. 1 Enoch fills the gap: he was hidden with the angels.
b: Genesis 5:24 says only: "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him." In Hebrew "walked with God" ('et-ha'elohim) can also mean "walked with the divine beings," and 12:2 takes it that way: all his work was with the holy ones and the Watchers. Jubilees 4:21–23 also says he was with the angels and wrote down what he saw. Hebrews 11:5 says he was taken "so that he did not see death."

a: Enoch the scribe
p: In the Second Temple period a scribe was a learned man of writing and the law. Enoch is the first.
b: Ṣäḥafi (Greek grammateus) is the title of Ezra, "a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6). Enoch is "the scribe of righteousness" (12:4; 15:1), the writer of books from heaven. Jubilees 4:17 calls him the first human to learn writing. The title shows who wrote and read these books: a circle of learned scribes who saw Enoch as their model.

a: who left high heaven, the holy and eternal place
p: Jude 6 uses nearly the same words: they "deserted the dwelling that was theirs."
b: Agrees closely: Jude 6 speaks of angels "who did not keep their own position but deserted the dwelling that was theirs." 1 Enoch 12:4 and 15:3 say the Watchers "left high heaven." Both treat leaving one's God-given place as the sin itself, linked to sexual sin, as Jude 7 then shows with Sodom. Bauckham and most commentators take Jude 6 as a summary of this passage.

a: They made themselves unclean with women
p: The language of uncleanness is the language of priests. Heaven is a temple, and the Watchers left it.
b: "Made themselves unclean" is the word the law uses for priests who defile themselves (Leviticus 21:1–15). In chapter 14 heaven is pictured as a temple with an outer and inner house, and the angels as its priests. Suter and Nickelsburg argued that the story criticizes Jerusalem priests who married women forbidden to them; compare Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13:28–29. Others read the language only as part of the story's own world.

a: Because they delight in their children
p: The EOTC text and the Greek say the Watchers delight in their children; Dillmann's text has a negative.
b: The Greek of 12:6 (Charles counts it 12:5) reads "since they rejoice over their sons." The EOTC Ge'ez agrees. Dillmann printed a negative reading, which most later editors set aside. The point is the punishment: they will see what they love most killed (also 10:12; 14:6).

a: Enoch went and said to Azazel
p: The Ethiopic names Azazel. The Greek has "Azael."
b: Here the Gizeh Greek reads "Azael" and the Ge'ez "Azazel" (see 8:1). In 13:1 Enoch begins his task as a prophet sent to the fallen angels. The angel who was sent from heaven now sends a human with a message to heaven's rebels: the roles are reversed.

a: so that they might be forgiven
p: The Watchers ask for forgiveness and are refused. Christian teaching has said the same of fallen angels.
b: Agrees: Hebrews 2:16 says Christ helps not angels but Abraham's descendants, and 2 Peter 2:4 says God "did not spare" the angels who sinned. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the fall of the angels cannot be undone because they chose with full knowledge (Catechism 391–393). Differs: some early Christians, notably Origen, hoped that in the end all spirits, even the devil, might be restored (On First Principles 1.6), a view later condemned.

a: or even lift their eyes toward heaven
p: The tax collector in Jesus' parable would not even look up to heaven.
b: In Luke 18:13 the tax collector stands far off and will not even lift his eyes to heaven, and he goes home justified. Ezra 9:6 prays, "I am ashamed and humiliated to lift my face toward you." The Watchers share the shame but not the outcome: their petition is refused (14:4).

a: by the waters of Dan, in Dan, southwest of Hermon
t: Dan and the springs of the Jordan
p: Dan, at the foot of Hermon, was an old holy place. Enoch receives his vision there.
b: Tel Dan lies by one of the main springs of the Jordan, at the foot of Mount Hermon. Jeroboam set up a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:29), and archaeologists have found a large sacred precinct from Israelite times and later. Nearby Banias (Caesarea Philippi) had a shrine of Pan, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ (Matthew 16:13–19). Nickelsburg argued that this region was a place where visionaries received revelations, and that the Enoch traditions grew there.

a: I read their petition until I fell asleep
t: Visions in sleep at a holy place
p: Seeking a dream at a holy place was an ancient practice, called incubation.
b: In the ancient world people slept at shrines hoping for a dream from the god. Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:11–17) and Samuel's call in the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 3:3–10) have something of this pattern. Enoch reads the petition by holy waters, falls asleep and receives the answer in a dream (13:8).

a: Ubelseyael
p: Probably the town Abel-beth-maacah near Dan, with a pun on Aramaic "mourning," since the Watchers sit there weeping.
b: The Ge'ez ʾUbəlsəyaʾel and the Greek Ebelsata are usually explained (Milik; Nickelsburg) as forms of Abel, the town Abel-beth-maacah or Abel-maim just west of Dan (1 Kings 15:20; 2 Chronicles 16:4), which lies "between Lebanon and Senir" (Senir is Hermon: "the Amorites call it Senir," Deuteronomy 3:9). In place names ʾabel means "meadow" or "watercourse," but in Aramaic and Hebrew it also sounds like "mourning," and both witnesses say the Watchers sat there mourning. Genesis 50:11 makes the same pun with Abel-mizraim. The setting fits Enoch's vision by the waters of Dan (13:7).

a: to rebuke the Watchers of heaven
p: Enoch takes God's word to imprisoned angels: the closest model for 1 Peter 3:19.
b: 1 Peter 3:19 says Christ "went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison." In 1 Enoch a righteous man goes to rebellious angels and announces their judgment, not their rescue (13:10–14:7). Agrees with one reading: many scholars read 1 Peter 3:19 as Christ, the new Enoch, announcing victory over these powers (1 Peter 3:22). Other readings see the preaching as offering salvation to the human dead (1 Peter 4:6). See the note at 10:12.

a: with a tongue of flesh
p: Enoch speaks about heaven with an ordinary human mouth, the gift God gave every person.
b: 14:2–3 makes a careful claim: God gave all people speech and understanding, and gave Enoch the task of rebuking the Watchers. A human being, not an angel, delivers God's verdict on angels. Paul says something similar about believers judging angels (1 Corinthians 6:3).

a: the winds made me fly
p: This is the oldest Jewish account we have of a man taken up into heaven to stand before God.
b: Isaiah and Ezekiel saw God's throne (Isaiah 6; Ezekiel 1), but did not travel upward to it. Enoch is carried by clouds and winds through a series of houses to the throne. This becomes the pattern for many later ascent stories: the Testament of Levi, 2 Enoch, the Apocalypse of Abraham, Jewish Merkavah writings such as 3 Enoch, and Paul's being caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2–4), and John's call, "Come up here" (Revelation 4:1).

a: a wall built of hailstones
p: Wall, outer house, inner house: the plan of the Jerusalem temple, drawn in fire and ice.
b: Enoch passes a wall, then a great house, then a greater house where God sits on a throne (14:9–20). This matches the temple's court, holy place and most holy place (1 Kings 6; Ezekiel 40–42). The cherubim on the ceiling (14:11) recall the cherubim carved in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:29). The angels serve as priests, and some stand near God by night and by day (14:23). Hebrews 8–9 also speaks of a true heavenly sanctuary of which the earthly one is a copy.

a: as hot as fire and as cold as hail
p: Opposites together: the house is beyond anything earthly.
b: Nothing on earth can be both burning hot and freezing cold. The picture says that God's house is wholly other. Psalm 18:12–13 puts hail and coals of fire together before God, and Ezekiel 1:22 speaks of a dome "like awesome ice" above the living creatures.

a: a high throne
p: Wheels, cherubim and fire under the throne: Ezekiel's vision, joined with Daniel's.
b: Ezekiel saw a throne above the cherubim, with wheels gleaming (Ezekiel 1:15–28; 10:1–22). Daniel saw a throne of fiery flames, its wheels burning fire, with a river of fire flowing out from before him (Daniel 7:9–10). 1 Enoch 14:18–22 has throne, wheels, cherubim, rivers of fire and a white robe. Most scholars think Daniel 7 used 1 Enoch 14 or a source shared with it, since this chapter is probably older than Daniel.

a: The Great Glory
p: A name for God himself, drawn from the "glory of the LORD" that Ezekiel saw.
b: The Ge'ez ʿäbiy səbḥat and Greek hē doxa hē megalē name God by his glory. Ezekiel calls what he saw "the look of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (Ezekiel 1:28). The Testament of Levi 3:4 also calls God "the Great Glory" in the highest heaven. Using "Glory" in place of God's name shows a reverence that avoids saying too much (compare 2 Peter 1:17, "the Majestic Glory").
orig: ዐቢይ ስብሐት (ʿäbiy səbḥat); ἡ δόξα ἡ μεγάλη (hē doxa hē megalē)

a: whiter than any snow
p: The Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 wears clothes "white as snow."
b: Daniel 7:9 pictures the Ancient of Days with clothing white as snow and hair like pure wool. In Revelation 1:14 the risen Jesus has hair white as snow, and at the transfiguration his clothes became dazzling white (Mark 9:3).

a: no flesh could look at him
p: No angel or human can look at God, yet Enoch comes near the door and hears his voice.
b: Agrees: God tells Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20), and John says no one has ever seen God (John 1:18). Enoch sees the robe and throne but keeps his face down (14:25). Goes beyond: 1 Enoch lets Enoch go nearer to God than any angel may (14:21–24), a claim no book of the 66 makes for anyone except Christ (Hebrews 1:3–4, 13). Later Jewish mystics built on this; see the Parables at 71:1–17.

a: Myriads upon myriads
p: Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 5:11 count the host the same way.
b: "Thousands upon thousands waited on him, and tens of thousands of tens of thousands were standing before him" (Daniel 7:10). Revelation 5:11 has "ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands times thousands" around the throne. 1 Enoch adds a teaching: God does not need their counsel. Isaiah 40:13–14 asks, "What adviser of his has taught him anything?", and Paul quotes it (Romans 11:34).

a: Come here, Enoch, and hear my holy word
p: Like Isaiah and Ezekiel, Enoch is commissioned as a prophet in God's presence.
b: Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1–3 follow a pattern: a vision of God, the prophet's terror, God's call and a message to deliver. Enoch's call has all of these, but his audience is the Watchers, not Israel. Ezekiel too falls on his face and is lifted up (Ezekiel 1:28–2:2), as Enoch is (14:24–25).

a: You ought to plead for human beings, not human beings for you
p: Angels were meant to pray for people. Now a man is asked to pray for angels.
b: In 9:3–11 the archangels bring the cries of humans to God. The Watchers should have done the same. Instead they had to ask a human being to carry their prayer (13:4). God's reply turns the request around: the right order of heaven is that angels plead for people.

a: a life that never ends
p: Spirits who never die have no need of children: the same reasoning as Jesus in Luke 20.
b: Agrees closely: in Luke 20:35–36, Jesus says those raised from the dead "neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die any more, because they are like angels." 15:5–7 gives the same reason: God gave wives to mortals so that their race would continue, but did not give wives to the spirits of heaven, who never die. The debate: some take Jesus' words to rule out the Watchers story (angels cannot marry). Others say 1 Enoch agrees: angels were not meant to marry, which is exactly why the Watchers sinned.

a: will be called evil spirits on the earth
p: 1 Enoch says demons are the ghosts of the giants. The Bible never says where demons come from.
b: Goes beyond: the 66 books speak of unclean spirits and demons (Mark 1:23–27; Luke 11:24–26) but never explain their origin. 1 Enoch does: when the giants died, their spirits went out and became evil spirits. Jubilees 10:1–11 continues the story, and Justin Martyr (Second Apology 5) and Athenagoras (Plea 25) repeat it. Later Christian teaching mostly held that demons are fallen angels themselves (Revelation 12:9). That the evil spirits "do not eat" yet seek bodies (15:11–12) is close to Luke 11:24–26.

a: Because they were created from above
p: The Ethiopic says the giants were created "from above"; the Greek says they came "from humans."
b: The Gizeh Greek reads "because they came into being from human beings," and the Ge'ez "because they were created from above." Both are true of the giants, whose fathers were angels and whose mothers were human (15:8). The Ge'ez fits the next words, "their first foundation was from the holy Watchers," and the Plain follows it.

a: The spirits of the giants trouble the clouds
p: Both witnesses say "clouds," but many scholars think the original said "Nephilim."
b: The Ge'ez dämänat and Greek nephelas both mean "clouds," which makes little sense. Greek nephelas sounds very like Nephileim, the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4. Many scholars, following Charles, think a Greek copyist turned "Nephilim" into "clouds." The Plain keeps "clouds" because both surviving witnesses have it, but the line may have meant that the spirits attack the giants' own kind.

a: They eat no food, they do not thirst
p: The Greek has evil spirits that "eat nothing" but "thirst"; the Ge'ez denies the thirst too.
b: The Gizeh Greek reads "not eating food, but thirsting," which fits restless spirits who want bodies (Luke 11:24). The Ge'ez says "they do not hunger or thirst." The Plain keeps the Ge'ez, which is the base text, and the variant gives the Greek.

a: without facing judgment
p: Evil spirits act on earth until the last judgment, as the demons in Matthew 8:29 fear.
b: Agrees: the demons in Matthew 8:29 ask Jesus, "Have you come here to torment us before the time?" In 1 Enoch the giants' spirits may destroy freely until "the day of the end, the great judgment." Jubilees 10:7–9 adds that God let a tenth of them stay under Mastema, the chief of spirits, to test humankind. Revelation 20:10 places the final judgment of the devil at the end.

a: You knew a worthless secret
p: What the Watchers taught was a cheap, partial knowledge, not heaven's real mysteries.
b: The Greek calls it "a secret of no value" (exouthenēmenon). The angels had not been told the deepest things ("the hidden things had not yet been revealed to you"), yet they taught the little they knew and it did great harm. 1 Corinthians 2:6–8 speaks of a hidden wisdom of God that "the rulers of this age" did not understand. 1 Peter 1:12 says the angels long to look into the gospel.

a: They took me to a place
p: Chapters 17–36 are a guided tour of the edges of the earth and the underworld.
b: Ancient peoples drew the world as a disk ringed by ocean, with mountains at its edges where the sky rests on the earth. A Babylonian clay map (the "Babylonian Map of the World," about 600 BC) shows this, and Greek writers such as Homer and Hesiod describe journeys to the ends of the earth and to the underworld. Enoch's journeys borrow this world picture and fill it with places of judgment and reward.

a: a river of fire
p: Greek myth had a river of fire in the underworld, Pyriphlegethon. Daniel has a river of fire too.
b: In Homer (Odyssey 10.513) and Plato (Phaedo 113–114), Pyriphlegethon, "blazing with fire," is one of the rivers of the underworld, and Oceanus circles the earth. Enoch sees a river of fire flowing into the great sea in the west. Glasson and others think the writer knew Greek ideas of the underworld; others point to Daniel 7:10 and Babylonian maps. Verdict: the writer seems to have used a picture of the world shared across the region, turned to serve Israel's God.

a: I saw the storehouses of all the winds
p: God asks Job whether he has seen the storehouses of snow. Enoch has.
b: God asks Job: "Have you walked into the places where snow is stored?" (Job 38:22) and "Who set down its corner stone?" (Job 38:6). The questions are meant to show that no human knows these things. Goes beyond: Enoch is shown the storehouses of the winds (18:1), the cornerstone of the earth (18:2) and the pillars of heaven (18:3). Agrees in purpose: both end in praise of the Creator (36:4; Job 42:1–6). Psalm 135:7 also speaks of the wind brought out of God's storehouses.

a: a stone called peka
p: The Ge'ez keeps a Greek stone name; the Greek has "antimony stone."
b: The Gizeh Greek calls the stone phouka, a word for antimony, the dark mineral used for eye paint (see 8:1). The Ge'ez peka copies the Greek. Isaiah 54:11 promises Jerusalem foundations set in antimony (Hebrew pukh) and sapphires: the same pair of stones as here. The throne of sapphire recalls Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:26.

a: There the heavens come to an end
p: The Greek says the heavens; the Ge'ez says the waters. The two words differ by one letter in Ge'ez.
b: The Gizeh Greek reads "the heavens were completed there." The Ge'ez text has "waters" (mayat), and "heavens" in Ge'ez is sämayat, so the difference may be one dropped syllable. The Plain follows the Greek because the next verses describe the edge of the sky (18:12, 14).

a: seven stars like great burning mountains
p: Stars that "broke God's command": Jude 13's "wandering stars" kept for darkness.
b: Agrees: Jude 13 calls the false teachers "wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever," an image that makes sense against 1 Enoch's punished stars (18:13–16; 21:3–6; see 86:1). Isaiah 24:21–22 says the LORD will punish the host of heaven and shut them in a prison. Differs: Psalm 148:3 and Isaiah 40:26 picture the stars obeying God completely. In the Bible stars stand for angels in Revelation 1:20 and 9:1.

a: because they did not come out at their proper times
p: Stars that run late: a warning to those who keep the wrong calendar.
b: The Enoch groups kept a 364-day solar year (see 72:1; 82:4–6) and accused others of following a wrong reckoning that put the festivals out of their proper times. Stars punished for not rising on time fit that concern. The Dead Sea Scrolls community kept the same solar calendar, and Jubilees 6:32–38 warns against the moon-based calendar.

a: ten thousand years
p: The Greek gives the time of the stars' punishment; the Ge'ez has "the year of mystery."
b: The Gizeh Greek reads "until the time of the completion of their sin, ten thousand years." The Ge'ez has "in the year of mystery" (bäʿämätä məśṭir). Scholars think a Greek number word was misread. 21:6 also has "ten thousand," so the Plain follows the Greek here.
orig: በዓመተ ምሥጢር (bäʿämätä məśṭir); ἐνιαυτῶν μυρίων (eniautōn myriōn)

a: to offer sacrifices to demons as if to gods
p: Deuteronomy and Paul say pagan gods are demons. 1 Enoch says the Watchers taught the worship.
b: Moses' song says Israel "offered sacrifices to demons, not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17), and Paul says what pagans sacrifice, they offer to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20). Psalm 106:37 says they sacrificed their children to demons. 1 Enoch traces this to the angels' spirits, which take many forms to lead people astray. Many early Christians, such as Justin and Athenagoras, held that pagan gods were these fallen spirits.

a: who led the angels of heaven astray
p: The Ge'ez blames the women; the Greek calls them only the angels' wives.
b: The Gizeh Greek reads "the wives of the angels who went astray," so the angels did the sinning. The Ge'ez reads "their wives, who led the angels astray." Chapters 6–7 blame the angels, who swore the oath and chose the women. The Ge'ez reading puts more of the blame on the women, as later writers such as the Testament of Reuben 5:5–6 did. The Plain follows the Ge'ez, since both readings are old, and the variant gives the Greek.

a: will become sirens
p: The Greek word is "sirens," the deadly singers of Greek myth. The Ge'ez misread it as "peaceful ones."
b: The Gizeh Greek says the women "will become sirens" (seirēnas). The Ge'ez has "peaceful ones," most likely from a misreading of the Greek seirēnes as eirēnaiai, "peaceful." The Greek Old Testament uses "sirens" for desert creatures that haunt ruins (Isaiah 13:21; 34:13; Job 30:29), so a Jewish reader would hear wild, ghostly beings as much as the singers of the Odyssey.

a: No human being will see as I have seen
p: Enoch claims a view of the universe no one else will have. John 3:13 says only the Son of Man came from heaven.
b: Conflicts, many think: Jesus says, "Nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven, the Son of Man" (John 3:13). Some scholars think this saying answers claims made for figures like Enoch and Moses. Agrees in part: the 66 books also say Enoch was taken by God (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5), without saying what he saw. The Ethiopian Orthodox church reads Enoch's claim as true prophecy; most other churches regard it as part of the book's literary voice.

a: These are the names of the holy angels who keep watch
p: A list of seven angels and their jobs. Tobit 12:15 and Revelation 8:2 also know "seven angels."
b: Raphael calls himself "one of the seven angels who stand in attendance and go in before the glory of the Lord" (Tobit 12:15), and John sees "the seven angels who stand in God's presence" (Revelation 8:2). The Ge'ez lists six names; both Greek copies close with "seven names of archangels," and the second copy adds the seventh name, Remiel (see 20:8). Here "watchers" is used in its good sense, the holy angels who keep watch (Daniel 4:13).

a: Tartarus
p: The Greek name for the deepest pit of the underworld, used in 2 Peter 2:4.
b: In Hesiod's Theogony (713–735), Tartarus is the dark prison beneath Hades where the Titans are chained. The Greek of 1 Enoch 20:2 puts Uriel over the world and Tartarus. 2 Peter 2:4 uses the verb tartaroō: God "threw them into Tartarus" and kept them in chains of gloom. The Ge'ez here has "thunder and trembling" instead, which the Plain does not follow (see the variant).

a: Michael
p: As in Daniel, Michael is the angel over God's people.
b: Daniel 12:1 calls Michael "the great prince who stands over your people," and Daniel 10:13, 21 shows him fighting for Israel. Here he is "set over the best of humankind," the righteous of Israel. Jude 9 calls him the archangel, and Revelation 12:7 has him lead the war against the dragon.

a: Saraqael
p: The Greek has Sariel, the name the Aramaic seems to give at 9:1 too.
b: The Ge'ez Säraqaʾel and the Greek Sariēl are two forms of a name that probably means "prince of God." In the Aramaic 9:1 as Milik read it, Sariel is one of the four archangels; in the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll (1QM 9:15–16) Sariel's name is written on the shields with Michael, Gabriel and Raphael.

a: Gabriel
p: Gabriel is in charge of the serpents, the garden and the cherubim.
b: The garden is paradise, and the cherubim guard it (Genesis 3:24). Gabriel, the messenger of Daniel 8–9 and Luke 1, is here its keeper. The Ge'ez has "the serpents, the garden and the cherubim"; the Greek "paradise, the serpents and the cherubim." The "serpents" may be the fiery seraphim (Hebrew seraph also means a fiery serpent, Numbers 21:6).

a: Remiel
p: The seventh angel appears only in the Greek. His charge is "those who rise," the raised dead.
b: The second Greek copy in the Gizeh manuscript reads, "Remiel, one of the holy angels, whom God set over those who rise," and adds "seven names of archangels." The first Gizeh copy also ends "seven names of archangels" but has only six names, so Remiel looks like the missing seventh. The Ge'ez lacks the verse. Remiel (perhaps "God's mercy" or "God has raised") appears in 2 Baruch 55:3 as Ramiel and in 4 Ezra 4:36 as Jeremiel. That an angel is placed over those who rise shows belief in resurrection here (compare 22:13).

a: a cleft in it that went down to the deep
p: A chasm of falling fire: the place Revelation calls the abyss and the lake of fire.
b: Revelation 9:1–2 opens the shaft of the abyss, with smoke like a great furnace. Revelation 20:10 throws the devil into the lake of fire. 1 Enoch distinguishes two places: the prison of the stars at the end of the earth (21:1–6), and this fiery chasm for the angels (21:7–10). Isaiah 30:33 speaks of a pit made deep and wide, with fire and much wood.

a: This place is the prison of the angels
p: 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 speak of this prison; 1 Peter 3:19 may too.
b: Agrees: 2 Peter 2:4 says God threw the sinning angels into Tartarus in chains of gloom, kept for judgment; Jude 6 has them kept in everlasting chains in darkness. Revelation 20:7 calls the abyss "his prison." Debated: 1 Peter 3:19 speaks of "spirits in prison" (Greek phylakē). The Greek of 1 Enoch uses a different word, desmōtērion, "place of bonds," here and in 18:14, but the picture is the same. See the notes at 10:12 and 13:10.

a: a great, high mountain of hard rock
t: The first map of the afterlife
p: Chapter 22 is the oldest Jewish text we have that divides the dead into groups before the judgment.
b: In most of the Hebrew Bible all the dead go to Sheol, a shadowy place with no reward or punishment (Psalm 88:10–12; Ecclesiastes 9:10). 1 Enoch 22 sets the dead in separate hollows inside a western mountain, kept apart until the judgment, with a bright spring for the righteous. This is a major step toward the later picture of a waiting place with rest and torment, as in Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31).

a: four hollow places
p: The Greek says "hollow"; the Ge'ez says "beautiful," probably from a misreading.
b: The Greek topoi koiloi means "hollow places," and the Ge'ez has mäkanat śänayat, "beautiful places." Greek koiloi (hollow) and kaloi (beautiful) look alike, and a translator seems to have misread them. The Plain follows the Greek here and in 22:3, since the next words describe deep, dark holes.
orig: መካናት ሠናያት (mäkanat śänayat); τόποι κοῖλοι (topoi koiloi)

a: four
p: The number of hollows does not quite add up: four in 22:2, "these three" in 22:9.
b: Raphael names four groups: the righteous (22:9), sinners not judged in life (22:10–11), the murdered who plead (22:12), and sinners who will stay there (22:13). Yet 22:9 says "these three." Many scholars think the chapter grew in stages, from an older picture of three divisions to four. The Gizeh Greek has a line the Ge'ez lacks: "three of them dark and one bright, with a spring of water in its midst" (see the variant). So the manuscript itself pictures one bright hollow for the righteous and three dark ones, which may be how the writer reconciled "four" and "three."

a: This is the spirit that came out of Abel
p: Hebrews 12:24 also says Abel's blood still speaks. Here his spirit pleads for justice.
b: God tells Cain, "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Hebrews 11:4 says Abel "still speaks," and Hebrews 12:24 contrasts Jesus' blood, which "speaks better than the blood of Abel." In 1 Enoch Abel cries for the end of Cain's line. Jesus links Abel to all the righteous blood shed on earth (Matthew 23:35).

a: here is the spring of water with light above it
t: The bright spring for the righteous
p: A place of light and water for the righteous dead: close to "Abraham's side" in Luke 16.
b: Agrees in picture: in Luke 16:22–26 the poor man rests at Abraham's side while the rich man thirsts in torment, with a great gulf between them that cannot be crossed. 1 Enoch 22 has separate places, light and water for the righteous, pain for sinners. Revelation 7:17 and 22:1 promise springs of the water of life. Differs: 1 Enoch's divisions are temporary, until the great judgment; churches differ on whether there is such an in-between state at all (see Purgatory in Catholic teaching).

a: Their souls will not be killed on the day of judgment, and they will not be raised from there
t: Not all the dead will rise
p: 1 Enoch 22 expects some dead to stay where they are, not raised at all.
b: Differs: Daniel 12:2 says "many" will rise, some to life and some to shame; John 5:28–29 and Acts 24:15 say all will rise, the righteous and the unrighteous. 1 Enoch 22:13 says one group of sinners, already punished in life, will not be raised. The Greek has "will not be punished" where the Ge'ez has "killed." The chapter shows Jewish ideas about resurrection still forming in the 200s BC.

a: the Lord of glory
p: Enoch's refrain of praise. Paul uses the same title for Jesus.
b: ʾƎgziʾä səbḥat closes each scene of Enoch's journeys (22:14; 25:3, 7; 27:3, 5; 36:4). Psalm 24:7–10 calls God "the King of glory." Paul says the rulers of this age "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8), and James speaks of "Jesus Christ, our Lord of glory" (James 2:1).

a: the fire of all the lights of heaven
t: The fire that drives the lights
p: Ancient science asked what moves the sun and stars. Here a running fire in the west does.
b: Greek thinkers argued about whether the heavenly bodies were fire, and what kept them moving. 1 Enoch places a restless fire in the west that drives or rekindles the lights. The detail fits the book's interest in the order of the heavens, worked out fully in the Book of the Luminaries (see 72:1).

a: seven glorious mountains
p: The middle mountain is God's throne: Zion and Sinai in one, at the edge of the world.
b: Isaiah 14:13 speaks of "the mount of assembly in the far north," and Ezekiel 28:13–16 places Eden on "the holy mountain of God" with precious stones. Psalm 48:1–2 calls Zion "in the far north" God's holy mountain. Enoch's seven mountains of precious stone, with God's throne on the middle one (18:6–8; 24:1–3; 25:3), join these pictures.

a: a tree whose scent I had never smelled before
p: Never withering, beautiful fruit, kept for the righteous: this is the tree of life.
b: The angel does not name it, but readers have always seen here the tree of life of Genesis 2:9 and 3:22–24, now kept on God's mountain until the judgment (25:4–5). Its leaves never wither, like the tree by the streams in Psalm 1:3 and the trees of Ezekiel 47:12. Revelation 22:2 places the tree of life by the river in the new Jerusalem, and its leaves heal the nations.

a: the eternal King
p: Nəguś zäläʿaläm, "King of eternity": one of the book's titles for God.
b: The Ge'ez nəguś zäläʿaläm (Greek basileus tou aiōnos) appears in 25:3, 5 and 7, and 27:3. Jeremiah 10:10 calls the LORD "the everlasting King," and 1 Timothy 1:17 gives glory "to the King of the ages." Tobit 13 uses the same title in a hymn to Jerusalem.
orig: ንጉሠ ዘለዓለም (nəguśä zäläʿaläm); βασιλεὺς τοῦ αἰῶνος (basileus tou aiōnos)

a: when he comes down to visit the earth with goodness
p: "To visit" is the Bible's word for God coming to act, in blessing or judgment.
b: The verb in Hebrew, paqad, and in Greek, episkeptomai, means that God comes to look after his people (Genesis 50:24; Ruth 1:6; Luke 1:68). Here God's visit brings goodness to the earth, and his throne stands on the mountain. Revelation 21:3 hears a voice: "Look! God's tent is with human beings."

a: no flesh has the right to touch it until the great judgment
t: The tree of life kept for later
p: Genesis closes the way to the tree of life. 1 Enoch says it will be opened again.
b: Agrees: in Genesis 3:22–24 God sets cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life. Revelation 2:7 promises the one who overcomes "to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God," and Revelation 22:14 says the faithful will have the right to it. Differs in detail: 1 Enoch plants the tree by the temple in Jerusalem (25:5) and gives a long earthly life (25:6). Revelation sets it in the new Jerusalem in a new creation, with no more death (Revelation 21:4).

a: It will be planted toward the north, in the holy place
p: Both witnesses say "north"; Charles changed it to "food."
b: The Gizeh Greek and the Ge'ez agree that the tree will be planted "toward the north," and the holy place is the temple. Charles proposed changing the Greek eis borrhan, "toward the north," to eis boran, "for food." Other editors, such as Nickelsburg, keep "north," since Zion is called "the far north" in Psalm 48:2 and the temple's altar stood on its north side (Leviticus 1:11).

a: as your fathers lived
p: The righteous will live as long as the patriarchs before the Flood.
b: Genesis 5 lists lives of over 900 years. Isaiah 65:20–22 promises that in the new creation a person who dies at 100 will be thought a child. 1 Enoch 25:6 promises that same long life after the judgment. See the note on 5:9.

a: the middle of the earth
t: Jerusalem, the center of the world
p: The blessed place in the middle of the earth is Jerusalem.
b: Ezekiel 5:5 says God set Jerusalem "in the middle of the nations," and 38:12 says Israel's people "live at the center of the earth" (Hebrew tabbur, "navel"). Jubilees 8:19 calls Mount Zion "the center of the navel of the earth." The geography in 26:2–5 matches Jerusalem: the holy mountain (Zion), the Gihon spring on its east flowing south, the Mount of Olives to the east, a lower hill to the west, and the deep valleys between: the Kidron, the Tyropoeon and the Hinnom.

a: sprouted from a tree that had been cut down
p: Isaiah's picture of a cut-down tree that sprouts again: Israel's hope after judgment.
b: Isaiah 11:1 promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and Isaiah 6:13 says the holy seed is the stump that remains when the tree is cut down. Job 14:7 says that a cut tree may sprout again. Enoch sees living branches growing from a felled tree in Jerusalem: life after judgment.

a: this valley between them is cursed
p: The cursed valley next to Jerusalem is the Valley of Hinnom: the Gehenna of Jesus' warnings.
b: The Valley of Hinnom (Hebrew Ge-Hinnom) south of Jerusalem was where kings burned children to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32). Jeremiah called it the Valley of Slaughter, and Isaiah 66:24 pictures corpses outside the city where the fire is never quenched. Agrees: 1 Enoch 27 makes this valley the place where the cursed are judged in sight of the righteous. Jesus uses "Gehenna" for final punishment (Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43–48), quoting Isaiah 66:24. Differs: 1 Enoch sets the punishment in an actual valley by Jerusalem; the New Testament does not give it a map.

a: says harsh things about his glory
p: The cursed are those who speak against God: the sin named in 5:4 and in Jude 15.
b: As in 5:4 and 1:9, the sin singled out is speech against God. Jude 15 ends his quotation with "all the harsh words ungodly sinners spoke against him," and Jude 16 describes grumblers whose mouths speak puffed-up words. Jesus says people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36).

a: the sight of a righteous judgment on them will be shown before the righteous
p: The righteous will see the punishment of the wicked. Isaiah 66:24 ends the same way.
b: Agrees: Isaiah's last verse says the worshipers "will go out and look at the corpses" of the rebels (Isaiah 66:24). Revelation 14:10 places the torment "in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb." Differs in spirit: in 1 Enoch the righteous bless God for his mercy as they watch (27:4); Ezekiel 33:11 says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and Jesus tells his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44).

a: the desert
p: The Greek writes a place name, Mandobara; it is the Aramaic for "desert."
b: The Gizeh Greek has "into the middle of Mandobara" here and "in Babdera" in 29:1. Both look like forms of the Aramaic madbera, "the desert," left untranslated. The Ge'ez keeps a related loanword too, mädbära (28:1; 29:1), which the Plain renders "the desert." East of Jerusalem lies the Judean desert, which runs down to the Jordan valley and the Dead Sea, as the route here does.

a: It looked like a great stream flowing toward the northwest
p: The Ethiopic joins this verse to 28:2. The Greek keeps it separate.
b: The Ge'ez manuscripts run 28:2 and 28:3 together, but the Greek counts them as separate, and the Plain follows that verse division. Water in the desert east of Jerusalem recalls Ezekiel 47:1–12, where a river flows from the temple to the Dead Sea and makes it fresh, and Joel 3:18.

a: trees of judgment
p: The phrase is obscure in both the Ge'ez and the Greek.
b: The Ge'ez says ʿəḍäwä kʷənane and the Greek kriseōs dendra: both mean "trees of judgment." Why spice trees should be called that is unclear; some scholars suggest that a word for a kind of spice-bearing tree was misread early on. The Greek also says the trees were "like nut trees," where the Ge'ez says they were "not like one another." The Plain keeps the Ge'ez and marks the doubt.

a: frankincense and myrrh
p: Frankincense and myrrh came from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa.
b: Frankincense and myrrh are tree resins from southern Arabia, Somalia and Ethiopia. They were burned in the temple (Exodus 30:34) and brought as gifts to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11). Chapters 28–32 follow the spice route east, with cinnamon, mastic, nard and pepper, toward paradise, which was thought to lie in the east (Genesis 2:8).
r: Exodus 30:34; Matthew 2:11; Song of Songs 4:14; Genesis 2:8

a: called sarira and galbanum
p: Two resins. Galbanum was part of the temple incense.
b: Galbanum is a strong-smelling gum named among the spices of the holy incense in Exodus 30:34. Sarira is a Ge'ez form of a word for a resin, perhaps storax. The Greek calls it "nectar, called sarran and galbanum." These spices tie the journey east to the temple, and the temple to paradise.

a: the Red Sea
p: The Greek says "the Erythraean Sea": the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean together.
b: For Greek writers the "Erythraean (red) Sea" meant the whole sea south and east of Arabia, including the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean. Enoch crosses it toward the far east and paradise. The Septuagint uses the same name for the sea of the exodus (Exodus 15:4), but here it is the ocean on the way to the east.

a: the angel Zotiel
p: An angel named only here. The Greek has the name without "angel."
b: The Ge'ez says Enoch "passed over the angel Zuṭel"; the Gizeh Greek has "I passed over Zōtiel," without the word "angel." No other text names him. He may be a guard placed at the edge of paradise, like the cherubim of Genesis 3:24, or the Greek may have meant a place, which the Ethiopic translator took for an angel because of the ending -el.

a: the Garden of Righteousness
p: Eden, far to the east, where the righteous dead and Enoch himself later dwell.
b: Genesis 2:8 places the garden "in Eden, in the east." 1 Enoch calls it the Garden of Righteousness; later parts say Enoch was taken there (see 60:8; 70:3; 106:8) and the Dream Visions also place him in paradise (see 87:3). Jesus promises the thief, "today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), and Paul was caught up into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:4).

a: the tree of wisdom
p: Genesis calls it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. 1 Enoch calls it the tree of wisdom.
b: Agrees: 32:6 tells the Genesis story: Adam and Eve ate, learned, their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and they were driven out (Genesis 3:6–7, 23). Differs: Genesis does not call the tree good to eat from, but says the woman saw it was "desirable for gaining wisdom" (Genesis 3:6). 1 Enoch keeps the tree in the far east and gives it a plain name, the tree of wisdom. It is the only mention of Adam and Eve in the Book of the Watchers, which puts the main blame for evil on the Watchers (see 9:9).

a: It looks like a carob tree
p: The Greek compares the leaves to the carob's (keratia). Its pods fed the prodigal son's pigs.
b: The carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a common evergreen of the eastern Mediterranean, with long brown pods. In the Gizeh Greek the tree is as tall as a pine and its leaves are like the carob's (keratia); the pine clause has no Ethiopic parallel, and the shorter Ge'ez compares the tree itself. The prodigal son longed to eat the carob pods the pigs ate (Luke 15:16). A homely tree for so great a fruit.

a: their eyes were opened
p: Raphael tells the Eden story in Genesis's own words.
b: Genesis 3:7: "The eyes of the two of them were opened, and they realized they were naked." 1 Enoch keeps the words, calling Adam and Eve "your father of long ago and your mother of long ago." Genesis 3:23–24 has God drive them out of the garden.

a: the gates of heaven were open
p: Ancient astronomy pictured the sky as a dome with gates at its rim for the sun, stars and winds.
b: In many ancient pictures of the world, the dome of the sky rests on the earth's edge, and the sun, moon and stars come out through gates or windows in its rim. The Book of the Luminaries works out these gates in detail (see 72:2–3), and the winds' gates in 76:1–14. Here Enoch sees gates in the east, north, west and south (33–36), a first sketch of that system.

a: I wrote down all their exits
p: Enoch the scribe makes the first book of astronomy, with an angel's help.
b: Uriel shows Enoch the stars, and both write: Enoch writes their exits (33:3), and Uriel writes their names and laws (33:4). The scene points ahead to the Book of the Luminaries (see 72:1; 82:1), which claims to be that record. Jubilees 4:17 says Enoch wrote down the signs of heaven in order, so that people would know the seasons.

a: cold, hail, frost, snow, dew and rain
p: Job and the Psalms see God bringing weather out of his storehouses.
b: "Have you walked into the places where snow is stored?" (Job 38:22). Psalm 147:16–18 says God gives snow like wool and sends out his word to melt it. Enoch sees that some winds bring blessing and some hardship (34:3), as Deuteronomy 28:12, 22–24 sets rain for blessing and drought for curse.

a: so that they would praise his work and all his creation
p: The book of journeys ends where the Psalms do: in praise.
b: Psalm 104 surveys the winds, waters, mountains and lights, and ends, "Bless the LORD, my soul" (Psalm 104:35). Psalm 148 calls angels, stars, snow and winds to praise. Enoch's journeys end the same way: he blesses the Lord of glory for works shown to angels and humans alike. Revelation 4:11 sings, "You created all things."
